triage.name: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD)
triage.reason: Diagnosis made by history of impaired control, craving, tolerance and withdrawal; common and high-yield for interview skills.

demographics: Men are roughly twice as likely as women to meet criteria for AUD
Prevalence is highest in adults under 40 and declines somewhat with age
Higher rates are reported in some American Indian/Alaska Native and White populations and in people with lower income or less education
Sexual and gender minority adults report higher rates of heavy drinking

risk_factors.text: Family history of AUD in a first-degree relative
Binge drinking (5 or more drinks for men, 4 or more for women in about 2 hours)
Depression, anxiety, PTSD or another psychiatric condition
Childhood trauma or adverse childhood experiences
Easy access to alcohol, peer or workplace drinking culture

family_history: Alcohol use disorder in a parent or sibling
Depression or anxiety in the family
Other substance use disorder in the family
social_history: Drinks most days or in heavy weekend binges
Has driven after drinking or had other alcohol-related injuries
Missed work or school because of drinking or hangovers
Lives alone or has limited social support
Financial or legal problems related to drinking
exposures: Work or social settings where heavy drinking is normal

chief_complaints.text: I drink more than I should and I can't seem to cut back
My family keeps telling me my drinking is a problem
I wake up shaky and sweaty and need a drink to steady myself
I've been feeling down and anxious and drinking to cope
I blacked out again last weekend
My stomach hurts and I've been throwing up

hpi.onset: Usually gradual over years, often starting with regular drinking in the late teens or twenties and escalating after a stressor, loss, or new social setting
hpi.duration: Typically years; the pattern of heavy drinking usually has been present for at least 12 months before criteria are met
hpi.progression: Drinking amounts and frequency creep upward, tolerance develops, and the person starts to lose control over how much they drink; attempts to stop bring withdrawal symptoms and repeated relapses
hpi.quality: A pattern of drinking more than intended, strong urges to drink, and time spent drinking or recovering
hpi.severity: Ranges from mild (a few criteria) to severe with daily drinking, blackouts, withdrawal, and medical complications
hpi.timing: Often daily or near-daily; some people binge on weekends or in episodes lasting days
aggravating: Being around other people who drink
relieving: Brief periods of abstinence, often followed by relapse

associated_symptoms.text: Drinking more or longer than planned
Strong craving or urge to drink
Needing more alcohol to get the same effect (tolerance)
Shakiness, sweating, nausea or trouble sleeping when not drinking (withdrawal)
Blackouts or memory gaps after drinking
Spending less time on hobbies, work or family because of drinking
Continued drinking despite knowing it is harming health, mood or relationships
Morning drinking or drinking to relieve withdrawal
Drinking while driving or in other risky situations
Failed attempts to cut down or quit
Irritability, anxiety or low mood between drinks
Seeing or hearing things that are not there during withdrawal

pertinent_negatives: No history of drinking in the morning every day from the start (early morning drinking suggests more severe dependence)
No history of mania or psychosis unrelated to alcohol
No abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting (would suggest pancreatitis)

positives.text: Anxiety or irritability when not drinking

argues_against: Psychosis or mania independent of alcohol use

positives.text: Nausea or vomiting in the morning

negatives: Severe right upper quadrant pain with fever

positives.text: Numbness or tingling in the feet
Yellowing of the eyes or skin

negatives: Spider veins on the chest and face

atypical.how_it_differs: They often drink less overall but still meet criteria; they may present with falls, confusion, insomnia, or worsening heart failure rather than obvious intoxication, and they reach higher blood alcohol levels with smaller amounts.

Patients often minimize or hide drinking because of stigma; they may present for prenatal care with poor weight gain, preterm contractions, or fetal growth concerns rather than asking for help with alcohol.
Adolescents usually binge drink episodically rather than drink daily; they present with school problems, injuries, or mood changes, and withdrawal is uncommon.
Patients with cirrhosis may report much lower intake because they feel intoxicated quickly, and they can present with confusion, bleeding, or abdominal swelling rather than craving.

general.mild: Well-appearing, alert, no distress; may smell of alcohol or have mild tremor
general.moderate: Restless, mildly tremulous, diaphoretic, appears anxious or irritable
general.severe: Ill-appearing, visibly shaking, sweating, agitated or drowsy; may be disoriented
general.critical: Toxic or obtunded, unresponsive to voice, or actively seizing; may be hypotensive and tachycardic

findings.maneuver: Note the odor of the breath during the interview

labs.caveat: Macrocytosis from chronic alcohol use, folate deficiency, or liver disease; normal in early or binge-pattern drinking.
Sensitive for recent heavy drinking but not specific; also rises with other liver disease and with many medications.
AST:ALT ratio above 2 suggests alcohol-associated liver injury.
Rises with advanced alcohol-associated liver disease.
Thrombocytopenia from alcohol marrow suppression, folate deficiency, or portal hypertension with hypersplenism.
Anemia from marrow suppression, folate deficiency, or GI blood loss.
Low folate is common with heavy drinking and contributes to macrocytic anemia.
Can be low with poor nutrition; check before attributing macrocytosis to alcohol alone.
Hypomagnesemia is common and lowers the seizure threshold during withdrawal.
Hypophosphatemia can drop sharply during refeeding.
Low from vomiting, poor intake, and renal losses.
Hyponatremia can be from beer potomania, SIADH, or volume depletion.
Low bicarbonate with a raised anion gap suggests alcoholic ketoacidosis or concomitant toxic alcohol ingestion.
Hypoglycemia from depleted glycogen stores and poor intake; can be masked by intoxication.
Low albumin suggests chronic liver disease or poor nutrition.
Prolonged with advanced liver disease or vitamin K deficiency.
Order when epigastric pain radiates to the back or vomiting is prominent; alcohol is a leading cause of acute pancreatitis.
Thyroid disease can mimic or worsen anxiety, tremor, and palpitations.
Ketonuria with a raised anion gap supports alcoholic ketoacidosis.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Prolonged QTc
Peaked T waves with shortened QT when hypocalcemia is present
Nonspecific ST and T wave changes
Low-voltage QRS complexes with pericardial effusion or severe hypothyroidism

findings.text: Cardiomegaly or pulmonary edema suggesting alcohol-related cardiomyopathy
Cerebral atrophy with widened sulci and ventricles
Coarse hepatic echotexture with nodular contour suggesting cirrhosis
Mamillary body or medial thalamic signal change suggesting Wernicke encephalopathy
Corpus callosum signal change suggesting Marchiafava-Bignami disease

initial.why: Looks for macrocytosis, anemia, and thrombocytopenia
Assesses liver injury, nutrition, and synthetic function
Checks electrolytes, glucose, and kidney function; hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia lower the seizure threshold
Hypomagnesemia is common and must be corrected to control withdrawal
Order when epigastric pain radiates to the back or vomiting is prominent
initial.only_if: epigastric pain radiating to the back or persistent vomiting

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before treatment planning and imaging
Screens for urinary infection and ketonuria
Thyroid disease can mimic anxiety, tremor, and palpitations
initial.only_if: tremor, palpitations, or unexplained weight change

initial.why: Looks for tachycardia, QT prolongation, and arrhythmia in moderate to severe withdrawal
initial.only_if: moderate or severe withdrawal, palpitations, or chest pain

initial.why: Standard tool to grade withdrawal severity and guide treatment
Brief validated screen that quantifies unhealthy drinking

supporting.why: Sensitive marker of recent heavy drinking
Low folate contributes to macrocytic anemia and neuropathy
Check before attributing macrocytosis to alcohol alone
Assesses steatosis, cirrhosis, and portal hypertension
supporting.only_if: abnormal liver tests, right upper quadrant pain, or suspected cirrhosis

supporting.why: Rules out intracranial bleeding or mass
supporting.only_if: head trauma, focal neurologic deficit, or new confusion

supporting.why: Evaluates aspiration, pneumonia, or heart failure
supporting.only_if: cough, fever, hypoxemia, or suspected aspiration

not_indicated.why: No role in the evaluation of alcohol use disorder
Not needed unless infection is suspected
Reserved for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy or other structural disease
Not routine; order only for trauma, focal deficit, or new confusion
Not routine; order only for respiratory symptoms or suspected aspiration
Not routine; order only for abnormal liver tests or suspected cirrhosis

decision_points: Assess for withdrawal severity with CIWA-Ar and treat before complications such as seizures or delirium tremens develop
Check pregnancy status before treatment planning and imaging in anyone who could be pregnant
Give thiamine before or with glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Correct magnesium, potassium, and phosphorus to reduce withdrawal seizures and arrhythmias
Screen for depression, anxiety, and suicide risk, and reassess after a period of abstinence

criteria.name: Alcohol use disorder, clinical criteria
criteria.summary: A problematic pattern of drinking causing distress or impairment, with at least two of the following in the past year: drinking more or longer than intended; wanting to cut down or unsuccessful attempts; spending a lot of time drinking or recovering; craving; drinking interfering with work, school, or family; continuing despite relationship problems; giving up important activities; drinking in hazardous situations; continuing despite knowing it worsens a physical or psychological problem; tolerance; and withdrawal. Two to three criteria indicate mild, four to five moderate, and six or more severe disorder.
items: Drinking more or longer than intended
Persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down
Much time spent drinking or recovering
Craving or strong urge to drink
Failure to fulfill major role obligations
Continued drinking despite social or interpersonal problems
Continued drinking despite physical or psychological problems

differential.name: Alcohol intoxication
differential.why_considered: Acute drinking episode with slurred speech, ataxia, and disinhibition that can look like the impaired control of AUD

history: Single episode or recent binge rather than a chronic pattern
No craving or withdrawal between episodes
exam: Slurred speech, ataxia, nystagmus that resolve as alcohol clears
No tremor or diaphoresis once sober
labs: Blood alcohol level correlates with exam findings
Normal MCV, GGT, and liver tests in isolated episodes

differential.name: Sedative-hypnotic or benzodiazepine use disorder
differential.why_considered: Same picture of tolerance, withdrawal, and impaired control with a different substance

history: Prescription or illicit benzodiazepine, barbiturate, or sleep aid use
Withdrawal with anxiety, tremor, and seizures similar to alcohol
exam: Sedation, ataxia, and slurred speech without alcohol on the breath
labs: Urine drug screen positive for benzodiazepines or barbiturates
Normal GGT and MCV

differential.name: Major depressive disorder
differential.why_considered: Low mood, poor sleep, guilt, and anhedonia overlap with AUD and often coexist
differential.trigger: Depressed mood, anhedonia, or suicidal thoughts that persist or predate heavy drinking

history: Depressive symptoms present during periods of abstinence and before heavy drinking began
No craving, tolerance, or withdrawal
exam: Flat affect, psychomotor slowing, no tremor or autonomic hyperactivity
labs: Normal GGT, MCV, and liver tests

differential.name: Generalized anxiety disorder
differential.why_considered: Anxiety, restlessness, and insomnia are common in both AUD and anxiety disorders

history: Worry is pervasive and not limited to drinking or withdrawal
Symptoms persist during abstinence
exam: Anxious but no tremor, diaphoresis, or tachycardia at rest
labs: Normal electrolytes, magnesium, and liver tests

differential.name: Alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens)
differential.why_considered: Severe autonomic hyperactivity, confusion, and hallucinations in a heavy drinker
differential.trigger: Confusion, fever, marked tachycardia, and hallucinations 48–96 hours after the last drink

history: Abrupt cessation after prolonged heavy drinking
Prior withdrawal seizures or delirium
exam: Disorientation, agitation, tremor, diaphoresis, fever, tachycardia
labs: Hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, low bicarbonate
Elevated GGT and MCV

differential.name: Hepatic encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Confusion, asterixis, and sleep-wake reversal in a patient with alcohol-associated liver disease
differential.trigger: Asterixis, disorientation, or drowsiness in a patient with known cirrhosis

history: Known cirrhosis or prior episodes of confusion
Precipitant such as GI bleed, infection, or constipation
exam: Asterixis, fetor hepaticus, jaundice, ascites, spider angiomata
labs: Elevated ammonia, low albumin, prolonged INR, thrombocytopenia
imaging: Coarse nodular liver with splenomegaly and ascites on ultrasound

differential.name: Wernicke encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Confusion, ataxia, and eye movement abnormalities in a malnourished heavy drinker
differential.trigger: Ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, ataxia, and confusion in a patient with poor nutrition

history: Poor oral intake, vomiting, and heavy drinking
Recent carbohydrate load without thiamine
exam: Horizontal nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, gait ataxia, confusion
labs: Low magnesium and low thiamine
Macrocytic anemia
imaging: Mamillary body or medial thalamic signal change on MRI

differential.name: Acute pancreatitis
differential.why_considered: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting in a heavy drinker
differential.trigger: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting

history: Constant severe epigastric pain radiating to the back
Nausea and vomiting without relief
labs: Lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal
Elevated AST and ALT
imaging: Pancreatic edema and peripancreatic fluid on CT

differential.name: Alcohol-associated hepatitis
differential.why_considered: Jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and fever in a patient with heavy recent drinking
differential.trigger: Jaundice with tender hepatomegaly and fever after heavy drinking

history: Heavy drinking within the past weeks
Anorexia, nausea, and right upper quadrant pain
labs: AST elevated with AST:ALT ratio above 2
Bilirubin elevated, INR prolonged, neutrophilia
imaging: Hepatomegaly with increased echogenicity on ultrasound

differential.name: Alcoholic ketoacidosis
differential.why_considered: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and tachypnea after a binge with poor intake
differential.trigger: Raised anion gap with ketonuria and low or normal glucose after heavy drinking

history: Binge drinking with little food for days
Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain
labs: Raised anion gap, low bicarbonate, ketonuria
Glucose low, normal, or mildly elevated

differential.name: Opioid use disorder
differential.why_considered: Impaired control, craving, tolerance, and withdrawal with another substance

history: Prescription or illicit opioid use
Withdrawal with diarrhea, yawning, piloerection, and mydriasis
labs: Urine drug screen positive for opioids
Normal GGT and MCV

differential.name: Bipolar disorder
differential.why_considered: Impulsivity, risky behavior, and heavy drinking during manic or hypomanic episodes

history: Distinct episodes of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, and grandiosity
Mood symptoms persist during abstinence
labs: Normal GGT and MCV

severity.mild: Two to three criteria met; drinking more than intended with craving and some role interference but no withdrawal or medical complications
severity.moderate: Four to five criteria met; tolerance and withdrawal are present, with continued drinking despite health, work, or relationship problems
severity.severe: Six or more criteria met; daily or near-daily drinking, morning drinking, blackouts, failed attempts to stop, and medical complications such as liver disease or neuropathy
severity.critical: Severe withdrawal with seizures or delirium tremens, or a life-threatening complication such as GI bleeding, pancreatitis, or alcoholic ketoacidosis

red_flags.meaning: Delirium tremens or Wernicke encephalopathy; needs urgent treatment and thiamine
Severe withdrawal; risk of further seizures and status epilepticus

red_flags.finding: Heart rate over 120 with fever and marked tremor

red_flags.meaning: Upper GI bleeding from varices, gastritis, or Mallory-Weiss tear

red_flags.finding: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back
Jaundice with tender hepatomegaly and fever

red_flags.meaning: High risk of self-harm; needs immediate psychiatric evaluation

complications.name: Acute pancreatitis
clues: Epigastric pain radiating to the back
Lipase more than three times normal

complications.name: Alcoholic ketoacidosis
clues: Raised anion gap, ketonuria, low bicarbonate

complications.name: Peripheral neuropathy
clues: Numbness and tingling in a stocking distribution

complications.name: Aspiration pneumonia
clues: Heavy drinking with vomiting and decreased consciousness

special_populations.differences: They may drink less overall but still meet criteria; they reach higher blood alcohol levels with smaller amounts and often present with falls, confusion, insomnia, or worsening heart failure rather than obvious intoxication.

Patients often minimize or hide drinking because of stigma; they may present for prenatal care with poor weight gain, preterm contractions, or fetal growth concerns. No amount of alcohol is considered safe in pregnancy, and withdrawal should be managed with close fetal monitoring.
Adolescents usually binge drink episodically rather than drink daily; they present with school problems, injuries, or mood changes, and withdrawal is uncommon.

Patients with cirrhosis may report much lower intake because they feel intoxicated quickly, and they can present with confusion, bleeding, or abdominal swelling rather than craving. Benzodiazepines for withdrawal must be dosed cautiously and thiamine given before glucose.
Electrolyte derangements and volume shifts are more pronounced; magnesium and potassium replacement must be monitored closely, and renally cleared medications need dose adjustment.

key_questions.question: How much do you drink on a typical day, and how many days a week?
key_questions.looking_for: Quantify in standard drinks; men over 4/day or 14/week and women over 3/day or 7/week exceed recommended limits

key_questions.question: Have you ever tried to cut down or stop, and were you able to?
key_questions.looking_for: Unsuccessful attempts or a persistent desire to cut down

key_questions.question: Do you ever end up drinking more or for longer than you planned?
key_questions.looking_for: Impaired control over how much or how long they drink

key_questions.question: Do you ever have a strong urge or craving to drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Craving, a core feature of AUD

key_questions.question: Do you need more alcohol than you used to for the same effect?
When you stop or cut back, do you get shaky, sweaty, nauseated, or have trouble sleeping?
key_questions.looking_for: Withdrawal symptoms; morning drinking to relieve them suggests more severe dependence

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a seizure or seen or heard things that were not there when you stopped drinking?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior withdrawal seizures or hallucinations; marks severe withdrawal risk

key_questions.question: Has drinking caused problems with your job, school, family, or friends?
key_questions.looking_for: Role obligations not met, relationship conflict, or giving up activities

key_questions.question: Have you driven after drinking or been in other risky situations while drinking?
key_questions.looking_for: Hazardous use such as drunk driving or unsafe sex

key_questions.question: Have you kept drinking even though it was making a health problem, depression, or anxiety worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Continued use despite physical or psychological harm

key_questions.question: How much of your day is spent drinking or recovering from drinking?
key_questions.looking_for: A great deal of time spent drinking or recovering

key_questions.question: Do you ever have memory gaps or blackouts after drinking?
key_questions.looking_for: Blackouts, which suggest heavier or more severe use

key_questions.question: Have you had vomiting of blood or black, tarry stools?
key_questions.looking_for: Upper GI bleeding from varices, gastritis, or a Mallory-Weiss tear

key_questions.question: Have you had severe belly pain that goes through to your back, with vomiting?
Have you felt down, anxious, or had thoughts of harming yourself?
key_questions.looking_for: Depression, anxiety, or suicidal ideation that needs immediate attention

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have a problem with alcohol?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of AUD in a first-degree relative

key_questions.question: How old were you when you first started drinking regularly?
key_questions.looking_for: Drinking before age 15, a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: What medications are you taking, including anything for sleep, anxiety, or pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Benzodiazepines, opioids, or sedative-hypnotics that add risk

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes counseling and treatment planning; no amount of alcohol is safe in pregnancy

reasoning_points: A problematic pattern of drinking causing distress or impairment, with at least two features in the past year
Impaired control: drinking more or longer than intended, wanting to cut down or unsuccessful attempts, craving, or much time spent drinking or recovering
Social impairment: failure to meet role obligations, relationship problems, or giving up important activities
Risky use: drinking in hazardous situations or continuing despite known physical or psychological harm
Severity is graded by the number of features: 2–3 mild, 4–5 moderate, 6 or more severe
Assess for withdrawal severity and complications such as seizures, delirium tremens, liver disease, pancreatitis, and Wernicke encephalopathy
Screen for co-occurring depression, anxiety, and suicide risk

easy: Classic daily heavy drinking with morning drinking, shakes, and blackouts
Clear failed attempts to quit and family conflict about drinking
Elevated GGT, MCV, and AST with an AST:ALT ratio above 2
Patient openly reports craving and withdrawal
medium: Binge-pattern drinking with normal liver tests and no daily withdrawal
Patient minimizes drinking; family brings up the problem
Co-occurring depression or anxiety that makes it hard to tell which came first
Older adult with falls and confusion rather than obvious intoxication
hard: Patient presents with a complication such as pancreatitis, GI bleeding, or withdrawal seizure and does not volunteer drinking history
Adolescent with school problems and injuries but no daily drinking or withdrawal
Pregnant patient who hides drinking because of stigma
Patient with cirrhosis who reports low intake because they feel intoxicated quickly
Confusion from hepatic encephalopathy or Wernicke encephalopathy rather than withdrawal
